definition: Generalize means to draw a broad conclusion from limited examples.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word generalize. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know generalize should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: One rude cabbie is thin grounds to generalize about a city of nine million.
Notice claims far less than generalize — one case, seen and reported, with nothing extended anywhere; to generalize is to stretch that single case over a whole class.
Stereotype goes further than generalize — a generalization can be tested and revised; a stereotype hardens into a fixed label that no new case can shake.

To infer is to reason to a conclusion from evidence, and the conclusion can be modest — one clue, one careful step. Generalize names one specific inference: stretching a small sample over a whole class. Every generalization is an inference; only the sample-to-class stretch earns the word generalize.

To universalize is to extend a claim to absolutely everyone — no exceptions, no borders. Generalize stops earlier: it stretches limited examples over some larger class, a school or a city, and the claim can still be tested and revised. Universalize is generalize pushed past every limit.

Generalize means to draw a broad conclusion from limited examples.
Three months into her exchange year, Priya's classmates back home wanted verdicts: what is breakfast like there, are the trains really silent, is everyone so formal?
She refused to generalize, typing the same reply — I have lived with one family, on one street, in one town.
She could describe her street perfectly; the whole country was a claim her one street could not carry.
Generalize is the exact word for what Priya refused to do, because generalize means to draw a broad conclusion from limited examples — stretching one household over sixty million people.
To infer is simply to reason from evidence, and can be modest; generalizing is the specific stretch from few cases to a whole class, and the smaller the sample, the thinner the stretch.
Generalize is the word for the move itself — sample to class — and it turns critical the moment the sample is thin: don't generalize is a warning about evidence, not manners.
Infer is broader and blameless; extrapolate, its technical cousin, extends a trend beyond the data.
When the stretch hardens about people, stereotype is the uglier word waiting one rung up this card's ladder.

Elena's first assignment at the food magazine was small: interview six diners at one downtown noodle shop and write up what she heard.
Her draft came back covered in red ink.
From six bowls of soup she had been happy to generalize, announcing what 'the modern city diner' wants, fears, and will pay.
Her editor circled the leap in one stroke: six people at one counter, stretched over a city of millions.
The correction stung, but it taught her the trade's quiet rule.
A finding may travel only as far as the sample that carries it.
Her next piece made the same visit and claimed only what she saw: six diners, one shop, one rainy Tuesday.
It ran without a single red mark.
